method_card.title: How to Factorise
steps: Always check for a common factor first: take out the HCF of every term.
For \(x^2 + bx + c\): find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.
For a difference of two squares \(a^2 - b^2\): write \((a + b)(a - b)\).
Check by expanding back to the original.
method_card.content:
Factorising is the reverse of expanding: rewrite an expression as a product of factors. Start by taking out the highest common factor of every term, for example \(6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3)\).

For a quadratic \(x^2 + bx + c\), find two numbers that multiply to \(c\) and add to \(b\); they fill the brackets \((x + p)(x + q)\).

A difference of two squares factorises as \(a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)\), for example \(x^2 - 16 = (x + 4)(x - 4)\).
method_card.example:
Factorise \(x^2 + 7x + 12\)

Step 1: No common factor across all three terms.

Step 2: Two numbers that multiply to \(12\) and add to \(7\): \(3\) and \(4\).

Step 3: \((x + 3)(x + 4)\)

Check: \((x + 3)(x + 4) = x^2 + 7x + 12\) ✔

problem_bank.bronze_description: Take out the highest common factor: the biggest number, and any shared letter, that divides every term.
problem_bank.silver_description: Factorise a quadratic x² + bx + c into two brackets by finding a pair that multiplies to c and adds to b.
problem_bank.gold_description: Harder factorising: take out a common factor first, then spot a difference of two squares or a perfect square.

bronze.title: Bronze: taking out a common factor
steps: Find the highest common factor (HCF) of the numbers in every term. If every term also contains a letter, that letter joins the factor.
Write the HCF outside a bracket, then divide each term by it to get what goes inside.
Check by expanding: multiply the bracket back out and you should land on the original expression.

silver.title: Silver: factorising \(x^2 + bx + c\)
steps: Find two numbers that multiply to c (the number at the end) and add to b (the coefficient of x).
Put them in two brackets \((x + p)(x + q)\). Watch the signs: if c is negative the two signs differ; if c is positive they match the sign of b.
Check by multiplying out: the two numbers should multiply to c and add to b.

gold.title: Gold: difference of two squares and beyond
steps: Always take out any common factor first, then look at what is left.
A difference of two squares \(a^2 - b^2\) has no middle term: square-root each part and write \((a + b)(a - b)\), one plus and one minus.
Check by expanding: the two middle terms cancel, leaving just \(a^2 - b^2\).

steps.content: \(x^2 - 36 = x^2 - 6^2\), a difference of two squares.
